title: Alarms, Fault Context and Maintenance Escalation

content.overview: Technicians do not need to diagnose every failure, but they must make faults legible. Learners practice building a time-ordered fault context, comparing current condition to expected baseline, performing only permitted operator checks, recognizing when resets are masking recurrence, and escalating without converting hypotheses into facts.

vocabulary.definition: A system indication that a measured or controlled condition met a defined alert or fault condition.
An observed effect of a problem that does not by itself establish the root cause.
Information about what, where, when, under what conditions and with what operational impact an equipment problem occurred.
Return of an alarm or abnormal symptom after it has cleared, reset or temporarily disappeared.

sections.title: An alarm is evidence, not a diagnosis
sections.body: A displayed alarm, abnormal sound, missing flow, high/low reading or leak is useful evidence. Similar symptoms can have different causes. Technicians capture the exact observation and context instead of assigning a root cause without supporting evidence.

sections.title: A timeline often matters more than a single snapshot
sections.body: Useful fault context includes the asset/location, baseline or prior status, first alarm time, recurrence, readings, permitted checks, process impact and safe actions taken. A time sequence helps the receiving maintenance or technical role reproduce the condition and distinguish intermittent from persistent faults.

sections.title: A reset is not a repair
sections.body: If a reset is explicitly permitted, completing it can be an operator action. When the same alarm returns, production impact continues or the procedure's retry limit is reached, repeated resetting can hide the persistent condition. Technicians preserve the alarm history and escalate rather than normalizing recurrence.

workedExamples: A pump alarm and dry zone are documented with asset, location, time and permitted checks before escalation rather than repeatedly reset.
An abnormal fan sound is reported with time, asset, operating state and observed change before the fan fails completely.
A permitted reset clears an alarm for five minutes and it returns; both occurrences and the affected zone are included in the fault timeline.
A high controller reading conflicts with a normal local gauge; the technician records both readings and instrument identities instead of choosing one as the root cause.
A maintenance ticket states 'possible flow restriction' as an unconfirmed hypothesis while keeping the verified no-flow observation separate.
commonMistakes: Resetting an alarm repeatedly to make it disappear.
Writing only 'broken' without asset, time, location or observed condition.
Declaring a root cause from one symptom.
Omitting the permitted checks already completed, forcing maintenance to repeat basic information gathering.
Failing to state crop/process impact or which area did not receive the expected service.
Opening protected equipment because the external checks did not explain the fault.
content.practicalApplication: Create a maintenance escalation from a simulated alarm packet containing equipment identity, prior status, time-sequenced alarms, controller readings, local observations, permitted operator checks and crop/process impact. Separate confirmed facts from hypotheses and identify the exact point where further work becomes servicing.
content.summary: Good fault reporting converts observations into actionable evidence. Technicians preserve the timeline, capture baseline changes and recurrence, complete only permitted checks, identify operational impact, and transfer unresolved diagnosis/repair to the authorized role.

blocks.title: Make the fault reproducible
blocks.body: The receiving technical role needs more than 'pump broken.' A strong escalation describes the exact asset, location, operating state, first symptom, recurrence, readings, permitted checks, affected process and controlled status. That context can be investigated without requiring the technician to guess the cause.

blocks.alt: Annotated maintenance-ready fault report showing asset and location, time, alarm or observation, permitted checks and results, process or crop impact, safe action and notification, with a warning against vague statements such as 'pump broken' and unsupported root-cause claims.
blocks.caption: A useful maintenance escalation gives the next qualified person enough context to reproduce and investigate the condition.

blocks.title: Observation, check, impact and hypothesis are different
rows: Observation
Zone 3 shows no flow at 14:10
Record directly with asset, location, time and relevant condition
Baseline change
Normal operating sound changed to intermittent grinding
State the comparison and when the change was noticed
Permitted operator check
Reservoir level verified normal under the operator SOP
Record the check and result without implying deeper diagnosis
Recurrence
Alarm reset at 14:12 and returned at 14:17
Preserve the sequence rather than recording only the latest alarm
Impact
Scheduled Zone 3 irrigation did not occur
State the affected process/crop area
Hypothesis
Possible internal pump or valve problem
Label as unconfirmed if useful and allowed
Root cause
Confirmed failed component/control logic
Belongs to the authorized investigation when evidence supports it

items.title: Identify asset and location
items.body: Use the exact equipment identifier, room/zone and affected process.

items.title: Record prior/baseline status
items.body: Note relevant normal condition, prior fault, maintenance status or recent change known from controlled records.

items.title: Capture first occurrence
items.body: Record time, exact alarm/symptom, readings and operating state.

items.title: Perform only permitted checks
items.body: Complete the operator checks explicitly allowed and record their results.

items.title: Capture recurrence or change
items.body: Record if the condition clears, returns, spreads or changes after an allowed response.

items.title: State process/crop impact
items.body: Identify what service, room, zone, material or schedule was affected.

items.title: Preserve safe status and escalate
items.body: Keep the asset controlled under procedure and hand the evidence to the authorized receiving role.

blocks.title: The reset clears the alarm for five minutes
blocks.setting: A pump alarm appears. One permitted operator reset clears it, but the alarm returns twice and one irrigation zone remains dry. The SOP does not authorize opening the pump or panel.
options: Keep resetting until the irrigation event finishes
Open the pump because the recurring alarm proves an internal blockage
Capture the recurring alarm and zone impact, complete only permitted checks, leave the asset/status controlled under procedure, and escalate with the fault timeline
Delete the alarm history after the reset succeeds
blocks.answer: Capture the recurring alarm and zone impact, complete only permitted checks, leave the asset/status controlled under procedure, and escalate with the fault timeline.
blocks.feedback: Repeatedly masking an alarm can hide a persistent condition. The technician should preserve recurrence evidence and stop at the operator boundary.

blocks.title: Two indicators disagree
blocks.setting: The controller reports high pressure, but a permitted local gauge shows a normal reading. No leak is visible. The operator SOP allows verifying both readings but not opening the system.
options: Assume the controller is wrong and continue
Assume the gauge is wrong and shut down every related system
Record both identified readings, time and operating context, complete the allowed checks, preserve the unresolved discrepancy, and escalate
Open the pressure system to determine which instrument is correct
blocks.answer: Record both identified readings, time and operating context, complete the allowed checks, preserve the unresolved discrepancy, and escalate.
blocks.feedback: Conflicting indicators are themselves useful fault context. The technician should not pick a root cause without evidence or cross into protected servicing.

blocks.title: Maintenance-ready escalation record
blocks.description: Capture facts that help the qualified receiving role reproduce and investigate the condition without requiring the technician to diagnose the system.

fields.label: Asset / location
fields.value: Exact equipment identifier, zone, room or work area

fields.label: Baseline / prior status
fields.value: Relevant expected state, prior fault or maintenance status

fields.label: Timeline
fields.value: First occurrence, resets/changes and recurrence times

fields.label: Alarm / symptoms
fields.value: Exact displayed alarm, sound, reading, no-flow condition, leak or other observed effect

fields.label: Relevant readings
fields.value: Permitted values/indicators including instrument identity when useful

fields.label: Process / crop impact
fields.value: What work, zone, material or schedule was affected

fields.label: Safe action / status
fields.value: Pause, out-of-service status, isolation where authorized or other controlled response

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: Optional unconfirmed idea clearly separated from observed fact

blocks.title: Turn a fault sequence into an actionable escalation
blocks.instructions: Use a simulated controller history, equipment ID, room map, readings and operator observations to create a maintenance-ready timeline.
prompts: Extract only facts directly supported by the packet.
Identify the baseline condition and first meaningful change.
List operator checks explicitly permitted by the SOP.
Show alarm recurrence and any reset history in order.
Separate reasonable hypotheses from confirmed observations.
State the exact point where further work crosses into servicing or hazardous access.
blocks.artifact: Maintenance fault timeline and escalation report

blocks.title: Remediation cue
blocks.body: If the report says only 'broken,' 'probably the pump,' or 'reset fixed it,' it is too weak. Add the asset, place, time sequence, exact symptom, permitted checks, recurrence and impact before claiming a cause.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Good technicians do not need to guess every root cause. They make the fault legible: what changed, where and when it occurred, whether it recurred, what was checked, what was affected, what safe status was preserved, and what remains for the authorized investigator.
